nameStory: The "water-crowfoot" name comes from the plant's distinctive underwater leaves, which spread out like a bird's foot with thin, thread-like divisions. The "yellow" part is obvious once you see those bright, shiny petals floating on the water's surface. "Crowfoot" was an old English term for plants with leaves that resembled a crow's splayed toes.
description: Yellow water-crowfoot is an aquatic buttercup that lives in ponds, slow streams, and muddy wetlands throughout New England. This perennial herb produces floating or creeping stems up to about 28 inches long that can root where they touch wet ground. What makes it fascinating is that it grows two completely different types of leaves - rounded, lobed ones above water and feathery, thread-like ones below the surface. The cheerful yellow flowers with their glossy petals bloom right at the water's surface or just above it.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Two distinct leaf types on the same plant: above-water leaves are rounded with short, blunt lobes that feel somewhat thick and waxy, while underwater leaves are divided into narrow, thread-like segments that feel soft and feathery when you gently run them through your fingers

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Bright yellow flowers with 5-8 (sometimes up to 14) glossy, reflective petals that shine like they've been polished with butter, each petal up to half an inch long, floating on or just above the water surface

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Stems float in water or creep along wet muddy ground, often rooting at points where they contact moist soil, creating sprawling mats in shallow water

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Small, dry fruits (achenes) clustered together in a dense, rounded head that develops after the flowers fade, similar to other buttercups but adapted for water dispersal

habitat: Look for yellow water-crowfoot in shallow ponds, slow-moving streams, marshes, and muddy areas around wetlands throughout New England. It thrives in both permanently flooded areas and places that dry out seasonally, often growing alongside cattails, sedges, and other water-loving plants. You'll find it from sea level up into mountain valleys wherever there's standing or slow-moving fresh water.

seasonality.spring: New growth emerges as water warms, with the characteristic two leaf types becoming apparent. Early flowers may begin appearing in late spring in warmer areas.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming season with bright yellow flowers most abundant from June through August. Both leaf types are fully developed and easily observed.
seasonality.fall: Flowers continue into early fall, followed by seed development. Above-water foliage may begin to yellow and die back as temperatures cool.
seasonality.winter: Most above-ground parts die back, but roots and underwater portions may persist under ice. Look for dried seed heads and remnant stem structures in ice-free areas.

funFact: This plant is like an underwater shape-shifter - scientists have discovered that the exact same genetic instructions produce completely different leaf shapes depending on whether the developing leaf is submerged or in air, and even the water temperature and plant hormones can influence the final leaf design!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with other aquatic buttercups, especially small yellow water-crowfoot, but yellow water-crowfoot is larger with bigger, shinier petals and more pronounced leaf differences between air and water forms. Remember: bigger blooms, bigger difference between the two leaf types.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called both "water buttercup" and "water-crowfoot," both names refer to the same plant - the buttercup family includes many "crowfoots" as alternative common names. Like other buttercups, all parts of this plant are mildly toxic if eaten, though its aquatic habitat makes accidental ingestion less likely.
compareHints: Among New England's many buttercups, yellow water-crowfoot is one of the few truly aquatic species, distinguished by its floating stems and dramatic leaf differences between air and water. Thread-leaved water-crowfoot has only the thin, underwater-type leaves, while most other buttercups in our area are terrestrial with consistently-shaped leaves. The glossy, relatively large petals and aquatic lifestyle make it unmistakable once you know what to look for.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's buttercups, small-flowered buttercup is unmistakable due to its tiny petals - all other buttercup species have much more prominent yellow flowers.
Among New England's buttercups, hooked buttercup is unique for its woodland habitat and tiny, pale flowers—most other buttercups prefer sunny, open areas and have much brighter, larger yellow blooms.
Among New England's many buttercup species, meadow buttercup stands out for its tall, upright growth and deeply palm-divided leaves.
Unlike meadow buttercup which grows in upright clumps, or bulbous buttercup with its swollen stem base, creeping buttercup is the only common buttercup that spreads by runners along the ground.
Among New England's many buttercup species, bulbous buttercup is the only one with that distinctive swollen stem base.
Unlike other New England buttercups that have bright, showy yellow flowers, cursed crowfoot has tiny, pale, almost insignificant blooms.
Among New England buttercups, bristly crowfoot stands out for its rough, hairy texture and pale flowers - most other buttercups have smoother leaves and bright golden-yellow blooms.
Among New England's buttercups, creeping spearwort is unique for its simple, narrow leaves - all other local buttercups have divided or lobed leaves.
Unlike the robust meadow buttercup or creeping buttercup with their typical three-lobed leaves, fen crowfoot has leaves so finely divided they look almost thread-like.

Among New England's many buttercups, early buttercup stands out for its combination of very early bloom time, preference for dry rather than moist habitats, and distinctively narrow, deeply-cut leaves.
Unlike the common meadow buttercup which grows tall and robust in fields, Allegheny Mountain buttercup stays much smaller and more delicate.
Rock buttercup stands out from other New England buttercups by having the smallest, palest flowers in the family - most other buttercups have bright golden-yellow blooms.
Among the 20+ buttercup species in New England, lesser spearwort stands out immediately because of its narrow, spear-shaped leaves – all other buttercups have lobed, divided, or rounded leaves.
Unlike the common meadow buttercup which prefers drier ground and grows much taller, swamp buttercup stays low and spreads along wet soil.
Among New England's aquatic buttercups, longbeak buttercup is distinguished by its exceptionally long fruit beaks and preference for flowing water.

Among New England's many buttercups, bristly buttercup stands out primarily for its rough, hairy texture - most other species like meadow buttercup and creeping buttercup have relatively smooth stems and leaves.

Unlike terrestrial buttercups like meadow buttercup or creeping buttercup, small yellow water-crowfoot is adapted for aquatic life with thicker, more succulent leaves and a strictly prostrate growth habit.
Unlike all other New England buttercups that grow upright, Lapland buttercup stays completely flat and creeping.
Among New England's many buttercups, water-plantain spearwort is unique for its completely undivided, lance-shaped leaves - most other buttercups have deeply lobed or divided leaves.
Unlike its terrestrial buttercup cousins that have typical yellow flowers, thread-leaved water-crowfoot has white petals with yellow centers and specialized underwater foliage.
